title: Nether Beast Character Study: Fake Natty, false Prophet
summary: First 'case profile' video: a long exposé of the YouTuber Nether Beast, whom NH argues was a fake natural with faked lifts and size claims, a cult-like in-group, an overpriced e-book and copy-pasted paid programs, and who preyed on sick people with herbal cures. NH uses the case to warn naturals about fitness-industry fakery, to argue that Nether discredited legitimate methods and the idea of pushing natural limits, and to tell viewers to value information over idolising personalities.

claims.claim: His 'case profile' series analyses YouTube fitness personalities; anyone whose real life is tied to their persona can ask him to delete a video about them and he will.
The Nether Beast research took about four months, tracking down mirror channels and private copies of deleted videos.
Nether claimed to be a natural man in his forties who had trained 20+ years with huge strength feats and a great physique.
Nether posed as anti-dogma and open-minded while rejecting anyone who disagreed: the tolerance paradox of being intolerant of intolerance.

Pathological liars can't give logical reasons for ideological choices and let the real reason slip: Nether hated the big three, especially conventional deadlifts, because he couldn't get into position, not because they're dangerous.
People without integrity find scientific-sounding reasons to justify personal bias against exercises they can't do.
Despite hating the big three, Nether chose them for his faked strength demos, admitting they are valid tests of strength.
Nether built a cult-like in-group in which accepting his ideas meant being open-minded and rejecting them made you a hater.
Every fitness YouTuber's audience forms an in-group to some degree: post a non-positive comment on a big channel and fans attack you without the creator lifting a finger.
An in-group that casts out critics is valuable for selling a product because no outside perspective challenges it.
Nether plugged his 50-dollar e-book constantly; if he truly wanted to help people as a health shaman he'd have released it for free.
His Q&As existed to sell the e-book: he got angry at repeated questions except the endless repeated supplement questions that let him plug it.
Anyone can fake their character on camera, but Nether's temper and sudden aggression slipped out repeatedly.
Nether's claims of a 900 lbs squat for 2, a 500 lbs bench and a 1000 lbs deadlift were obviously bogus to anyone who knows strength.

numbers.load: 900 lbs squat x2, 500 lbs bench, 1000 lbs deadlift

claims.claim: Nether's claimed 21-inch arms were impossible; NH's own leg is 26 inches, and Nether would have been lucky to have 17-inch arms.
Nether wasn't natural: he reviewed prohormones and said he took them. Once caught lying about one thing, someone can never be trusted again.
Later Nether lost about 40 lbs and looked like he didn't lift; losing everything when coming off is a sign of a fake natty.
If you need drugs to build an impressive physique, you know nothing about lifting, and such people shouldn't advise others on getting big.
Even enhanced, Nether's measurements were poor: a great back but ~17-inch arms and ~20-22-inch legs, the epitome of a torso-dominant physique with no limbs.
Fake natties like Nether hurt natural lifters who trusted them and make people believe impressive natural physiques are impossible.
NH shares Nether's stated beliefs that you can look amazing natural and push the limits, which makes Nether the perfect example of what he doesn't want to become.
When someone sells you the cure, they likely created the illness: Nether used his drug-built physique to make naturals feel inadequate, then sold the e-book as the fix.
Natural lifters are insecure because they're bombarded by images of enhanced guys who are bigger and stronger, which makes them easy targets.
Nether was easy to see through; people overlooked the red flags because they wanted to believe. If something is suspicious, call it out; blocking or refusing to answer is a red flag.
Ego drives every fitness channel, his own included: creators want appreciation for the strength or physique they built.
Claiming 20-30 years of training was Nether's way of explaining why followers didn't get his results, yet 2015 footage showed a normal-looking guy, so his mass came from PEDs.
The e-book is mostly links with almost no information.
Paid one-on-one consultations are fine in principle, but Nether sold 'tailored' programs that were copy-pasted templates, then sold a bundle of those same three templates.
Free templates are fine; charging for a 'specific' program and sending a cookie-cutter one is a scam.
Telling cancer patients to replace medical treatment with herbs and shamanic rituals is criminal; he has seen people die after following such scams.

From his calisthenics days: at 160 lbs he could do about two one-arm chin-ups, at 170 lbs none; a 240 lbs man repping them is implausible, and footage showed Nether jumping, using straps and doing quarter reps.
Nether was probably unemployed, so he needed the money and preyed on desperate people.
NH suspects Nether had untreated mental illness worsened by PEDs; his later soft-spoken demeanour suggests the earlier fire was exogenous testosterone.
Everyone wants to believe in something bigger; adulthood strips away the sense of magic, which is why religion persists and why people without belief aren't happy.
Finding one thing to believe in makes life worth living, but selling fake dreams to believers is wrong.
Nether discredited legitimate methods such as blood flow restriction and raw garlic, and the good information in his Q&As is now dismissed because of the fraud.
A superhero complex is fine if you stay real: NH lifts to look like an anime character but works to become that person rather than faking it.

YouTube fitness is powerlifting-centric; people badger you to squat, bench and deadlift, and that pressure pushed Nether to fake big-three lifts. NH refuses to do low-bar squats no matter how often he's asked.
Odd lifts and partials can mask true strength because nobody can compare them; his own 500 lbs front-rack holds look impressive but Olympic lifters do 700 lbs easily.
Nether chest shrugs put the shoulders in a compromised position and risk snapping a tendon; they are not a bench press replacement.
Liars who are exposed and simply flee are the epitome of YouTube fakery; an honest apology would have earned forgiveness.

Never trust anyone on YouTube fitness; watch knowledge channels for information, not to idolise the person. That's why he doesn't give his name and presents himself as an average guy who got there through hard work.
He sells nothing on his channel; the day he starts selling things, viewers should worry.
PEDs will not cure insecurities; you need to address mental issues another way.
